newsitem.title: UK: UK prompt natgas up on weekend flex buying and col.
newsitem.headline: UK prompt natgas up on weekend flex buying and col.

text.p: UK spot natural gas prices were firm in the prompt period on Monday following a flexibility mechanism system buy on Friday. But levels softened in the coming winter as one major seller was reported selling several pieces in the fourth quarter and the six month winter strip.

The flexibility mechanism had paid a system marginal price of 1.472 pence a KiloWatt hour (43.14 pence a therm) on Friday evening, with a system average price (SAP) of nearly 40.91 pence a therm, and this boosted the rolling average prices over both the 7-day and 30-day periods.

Transco said that on Sunday the 7-day rolling average SAP was 0.5127 p/kWh (15.03 p/th), and the 30 day SAP was 0.4133 p/kWh (12.11 p/th), even though there were 16 system sells on Sunday at a SAP of 0.2909 p/kWh (around 8.53 p/th).
It was the strength on the SAP that was cited by traders as the reason for the strength of prompt gas on Monday.

"It's a token observance of high SAP prices," said one trader who did a deal for 500,000 therms on the within day market at 11.80 pence a therm. Dealers added that unseasonal cold weather across much of Britain was also boosting heating demand.
There had been persistent rumours that terminal problems at Bacton, Theddlethorpe and offshore had contributed to the shortage which led to Friday's system buy and to the higher SAP as a result.

But Transco said the system buy was triggered purely by supply and demand fundamentals. "It was brought about by excessive demand and lack of gas available," said a spokeswoman, pointing out that gas demand had soared over the weekend as temperatures dropped.
Several players in the market said on Monday that any terminal and offshore problems appeared to have been resolved and there were no delays to gas flows during the day.

One trader said a further contributory factor to high day ahead prices on Monday was high bid prices on the electricity pool for Tuesday. This had made it attractive for some generators to increase their spot gas purchases to work the "spark spread" between gas and electricity.

Apart from the prompt period, there was significant activity next winter. One player reported involvement in six deals in either Q4 alone or the Q4/Q1 strip, and prices softened in Q4 on the back of some aggressive offers. But Q1 remained relatively stable, and the gas year from October was only slightly softer.

The IPE futures contract mirrored the falls over the winter. Only three trades were done, totalling 70 lots, with November softening to settle at 12.45 pence a therm, down 0.065 pence, while December softened by only 0.015 pence a therm to settle at 13.90 pence.
